claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or matched high-entropy derivatives have high saturation magnetization and coercivity at or below approximately 100 Oe.
The proposed intervention is adding approximately 1–5 at.% interstitial carbon to fcc FeCoNi.
Carbon addition will induce local lattice distortions in the fcc matrix.
Carbon addition may produce nanoscale precipitates.
Carbon-induced lattice strain will enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Carbon-induced lattice strain or precipitates will increase domain-wall pinning.
Enhanced magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain-wall pinning will increase coercivity.
Interstitial doping has enhanced coercivity through analogous behavior in other ferromagnetic alloys.
Carbon-doped samples will exhibit coercivity significantly above 100 Oe and above that of an undoped matched baseline.
Adding 1–5 at.% carbon will cause only minimal loss of the high saturation magnetization of fcc FeCoNi.
The intended intervention must retain the fcc matrix or phase.
Higher carbon concentrations may cause phase separation or excessive lattice strain.
Carbon-induced phase separation or excessive strain may compromise saturation magnetization.
Room-temperature hysteresis measurements on identically processed doped and undoped samples can directly test the predicted coercivity change.

contradictions.description: Nanoscale precipitates are offered as a possible beneficial mediator, while the experiment calls for phase purity and the boundary requires preservation of the fcc phase. If the precipitates constitute a distinct phase, these requirements conflict; the hypothesis does not distinguish coherent carbon-rich features from disallowed secondary phases.

The intervention explicitly changes composition by adding 1–5 at.% carbon, whereas the boundary says that the overall alloy composition must be preserved. This is inconsistent unless 'overall composition' is intended to mean preservation of the Fe:Co:Ni ratio rather than unchanged total composition.
